questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: The Three Components of an Attitude
questions.learningObjective: identify the cognitive, affective and behavioural components of an attitude
questions.stem: A survey separately asks whether recycling matters to someone, how they feel when they skip it, and how often they actually sort their waste. What do those three questions tap?

options.text: A belief, a feeling, and a tendency to act, which are the three components of one attitude
Three separate attitudes, one for thoughts, one for feelings, and one for actions, held separately
options.misconception: believes thoughts, feelings and actions are distinct attitudes rather than parts of one

options.text: The same component asked twice, since a question about feeling and a question about acting agree
options.misconception: believes the affective and the behavioural component are one and the same measurement

options.text: The attitude's strength, its direction and its persistence, which are three further components
options.misconception: confuses the three components with the three dimensions that an attitude may have

questions.explanation: The three components are a belief about the object, an emotional reaction to it, and a readiness to act, so a survey that asks about each is sampling three parts of a single evaluative response. What the behavioural component adds is awareness of how one behaves, which is exactly why a general feeling and a specific reported act can come apart. The tempting belief that thoughts, feelings and actions are three different attitudes fails because the three are defined as components of one construct rather than as rival ones. The belief that a feeling and a behaviour report the same thing fails because a general evaluation and a specific act are known to correlate only weakly, which is the whole reason the two questions are asked separately. The belief that strength, direction and persistence are further components fails because those are properties any single attitude may have, not the parts it is built from.
questions.hint: Ask what the three-part split in the definition of an attitude actually is.

questions.topic: Social Psychology: Attitude and Behaviour as Different Objects
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an attitude from the behaviour it might produce
questions.stem: A driver says in a survey that seat belts matter, then is asked openly about a friend who never wears one. What distinction does that pair of items probe?

options.text: An attitude is an internal evaluation, while a behaviour is the act that evaluation may or may not produce
An attitude is private and a behaviour is public, so the two can never be measured in one person
options.misconception: believes attitudes are always hidden and behaviours always openly observed

options.text: A behaviour is a past act and an attitude is a future intention, so they differ only in tense
options.misconception: confuses the attitude-behaviour distinction with a difference in time direction

options.text: A behaviour changes an attitude but an attitude never changes a behaviour, so one arrow only
options.misconception: believes causal influence runs only from acting to believing and never back

questions.explanation: An attitude is a summary evaluation held in the person, whereas a behaviour is something the person does in the world, and the two are measured with different instruments and correlate only imperfectly. That imperfect link is a real finding rather than a flaw, because situational constraints, habit and how strongly the behaviour is specified all sit between the evaluation and the act. The tempting belief that attitudes are hidden and behaviours public fails because a person can also report an attitude openly and can also act where nobody is watching. The belief that the difference is only one of tense fails because a past act and a future intention are not the same contrast as an evaluation and an act. The belief that influence runs one way only fails because behaving can and does change what a person then believes.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two is a summary evaluation and which is something done in the world.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: Naming the Discomfort of Inconsistency
questions.learningObjective: state what cognitive dissonance is and what it is a tension between
questions.stem: A person who values honesty has just lied to a close friend, and reports feeling uncomfortable without saying why. Which account names that discomfort?

options.text: Dissonance, the tension felt from holding two inconsistent cognitions about the same thing
Guilt, the fear a person feels when a lie is likely to be discovered by somebody else
options.misconception: believes the discomfort depends on being found out rather than on inconsistency

options.text: An argument, the clash a person has with the individual who was deceived by the lie
options.misconception: reduces the discomfort to an interpersonal dispute with the person harmed

options.text: Relief, the pleasure a dishonest person feels once an act has escaped any penalty this time
options.misconception: explains the discomfort as the opposite feeling, a sense of lucky escape

questions.explanation: Dissonance is specifically the tension produced by holding two inconsistent cognitions, here a stated valuing of honesty alongside a behaviour that contradicts it, and it is the inconsistency that is aversive rather than the act itself. The two cognitions in tension do not have to be equal in strength, so a person can be markedly more upset about a lie than a small hypocrisy. The tempting belief that this is guilt about discovery fails because the discomfort in the description appears with no one having found out, and it can be reported privately. The belief that it is an argument with the victim fails because the victim is absent and the tension is between the person's own two positions. The belief that it is relief fails because the feeling described is aversive, and a lack of consequence is what would make it feel like relief.
questions.hint: Ask whether the discomfort needs a witness, or only two inconsistent positions.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: Reducing Dissonance by Changing the Attitude
questions.learningObjective: identify dissonance reduction that works by revising the attitude
questions.stem: After a long drive a cyclist stops for a weak coffee, dismisses it as poor, and resolves to buy a better one next time. Which route to reducing dissonance is this?

options.text: The attitude to the coffee is revised to fit the act already completed, which is attitude change
The behaviour is revised in future, so the tension goes once the cyclist carries out the resolution
options.misconception: names future behaviour change as the route that dissolves present discomfort

options.text: A reason is added after the fact that makes the purchase look sensible, which is a justification
options.misconception: confuses revising the evaluation with bolstering the act by adding a reason

options.text: The tension is simply ignored, and it fades as soon as the cyclist stops thinking about the drink
options.misconception: believes mere inattention is a recognised way of reducing dissonance

The tempting belief that the future resolution is the route fails because a plan for next week does nothing about the inconsistency that already exists between the value and the completed act. The belief that a reason has been added fails because nothing explanatory was brought in, the evaluation itself was moved. The belief that inattention is a route fails because distraction can reduce the experience of discomfort without the inconsistency itself having been resolved, which is a different account from the one the item tests.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two inconsistent elements was still available for change.

questions.learningObjective: identify dissonance reduction that works by adding a post-hoc justification
questions.stem: A student who had to sit through a dull required lecture reports weeks later that it was more interesting than an optional lecture. Which account fits that shift best?

options.text: Attention, since the student has simply paid closer attention to the topic than before

The belief that a compulsory act produces no tension fails because the very feature that generated the ratings, having no free choice, is what makes the act hard to explain away. The belief about attention fails because nothing in the description says the student was more attentive, and attention would not by itself produce a preference for the duller option.

questions.topic: Social Psychology: Self-Justification Against Self-Handicapping
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an excuse made in advance from one built after the event
questions.stem: Before a graded talk a student picks a topic they find dull, and afterwards says the topic itself was boring. How should that sequence be classified?

options.text: Self-handicapping, since an excuse is selected in advance to protect self-esteem if the talk goes badly
Self-justification, since the excuse was built afterwards to make the finished talk look reasonable
options.misconception: confuses an excuse chosen in advance with one constructed after the event

options.text: Attitude change, since the student has honestly come to find a dull topic genuinely uninteresting

options.text: Confirmation bias, since the student gathered evidence that a dull topic deserved a low mark

The belief that it is attitude change fails because the dullness is being offered as the reason for a result, not adopted as a new preference. The belief about confirmation bias fails because there is no search for confirming evidence in the sequence at all, only a ready-made excuse.

questions.topic: Social Psychology: Locus and Stability in Attribution
questions.learningObjective: classify an attribution by locus and by stability
questions.stem: A supervisor watches a clerk misread a price ticket, then tells the clerk the mistake was careless. Which pairing does that judgement imply?

options.text: Locus internal, because the cause is placed in the person rather than in the surroundings
Locus external, because the cause is placed in the ticket rather than in the person who read it
options.misconception: reads a blaming judgement as one that blames the surrounding situation

options.text: Locus internal and stability unstable, because a single slip is judged a passing temporary mood
options.misconception: assumes that blaming a person also means judging them permanently changed

options.text: Locus external and stability stable, because that same ticket will keep producing the error again
options.misconception: assumes that a situational cause must also be a lasting cause

Stability is a separate dimension, asking whether the cause persists over time, and it is not settled by the choice of locus at all. The tempting belief that the attribution is external fails because the surroundings are exactly what the supervisor has discounted, not what he has blamed. The belief that blaming a person implies a stable trait fails because the two dimensions are independent, and a person can be called careless for one episode without the quality being held to be enduring. The belief that a situational cause is automatically stable fails because an argument runs the other way too: some situational causes are permanent features of the setting and some personal qualities are brief states.
questions.hint: Ask separately where the cause was placed and whether it was held to persist.

questions.topic: Social Psychology: The Fundamental Attribution Error
questions.learningObjective: identify discounting of the situation in favour of a disposition
questions.stem: Observers watch a manager cut off a speaker, decide the manager is arrogant, and never weigh that the speaker ran past a time limit. What is missing?

options.text: The situation was discounted in favour of the person's disposition, which is the standard error
The situation was used instead, since the time limit is itself a real constraint on the speaker
options.misconception: reads the observers as situational when they discounted the situation

options.text: Evidence was sought that fitted the first impression, which is a confirmation bias at work
options.misconception: labels a disposition-first judgement as a biased search for evidence

options.text: A correspondence bias, which applies only to observers watching very young children
options.misconception: confuses the general observer-side error with its child-specific form

That overweighting of disposition over situation is the error, and it is worth noting that a genuine constraint was present rather than merely possible. The tempting belief that the observers were situational fails because the time limit is precisely the fact their explanation left out. The belief that this is confirmation bias fails because no evidence was gathered at all here, the constraint was simply not weighed, and a search for supporting evidence is a different process from an unused situational cue. The belief that this is the child-specific form fails because the child-specific form concerns reading another actor's behaviour as a preference, which is a different judgement from an observer's trait inference.

questions.learningObjective: identify reading an actor's behaviour as a preference under visible pressure
questions.stem: A child watches one puppet hand coins to another, though a puppet standing above the screen is visibly calling the lines. What is the child being said to do?

options.text: Copy a rewarded action, since children imitate whatever act has just been paid for
options.misconception: explains the choice as imitation of a rewarded act rather than as an attribution

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: The Self-Serving Bias in Outcome Attribution
questions.learningObjective: recognise internal attribution of success and external attribution of failure
questions.stem: After a quiz, students who scored well cite the clear explanations, and students who scored poorly cite unfair marking. What is happening?

options.text: Good results are taken as internal and poor ones as external, which is the self-serving bias
Both groups put the cause outside themselves, so no self-serving split is present here
options.misconception: misses the split between the two groups' attributions

options.text: Both groups put the cause inside themselves, differing only in how generous the praise is
options.misconception: misses that the low scorers placed the cause outside themselves

options.text: The results are put down to the difficulty of the topic, so a topic effect explains both
options.misconception: reduces two different attributions to one shared topical cause

questions.explanation: The two groups made opposite attributions about the same event, which is what defines the pattern: the cause of a good outcome is claimed for the self, and the cause of a bad outcome is placed elsewhere. A pattern like this shows up in both individual and group accounts, and it is strongest where the outcome is seen as diagnostic of ability. The tempting belief that both groups went external fails because the high scorers cited explanations that were under their own control, such as preparing well, rather than anything about the paper. The belief that both went internal fails because the low scorers put the fault in the marking, which is not theirs. The belief that a shared topic effect explains both fails because a single topic effect would push the two groups towards the same attribution, and here they diverge on the one event they share.
questions.hint: Ask where each group placed the cause of the one event they all experienced.

questions.learningObjective: describe the just-world belief as a general attribution tendency
questions.stem: A driver who is cut off in traffic shrugs and says the other motorist was probably running late. What produces that reaction?

The self-serving bias, which hands credit for good luck to whoever happened to receive it
options.misconception: treats making an outcome explicable as a self-crediting attribution

questions.learningObjective: distinguish fitting in from believing the group is right
questions.stem: A lab member in gloves chooses between a small and a large tip for a short task, copying whichever option the other members chose. Which influence is that?

Informational influence, because the member is working out which tip is the accurate one
options.misconception: reads social copying as a search for the correct answer rather than for fit

options.text: Obedience, because a supervisor in the room is implicitly demanding the larger payment
options.misconception: mistakes a peer model for an instruction issued by an authority

options.text: Deindividuation, because the member has lost self-awareness inside the lab group

The tempting belief that this is informational influence fails because nothing in the situation lets a member learn the correct amount from the others, and a lab rule about tips would be a plausible source of real information if one existed. The belief that it is obedience fails because the description offers a supervisor doing nothing, and obedience needs a request directed at the person. questions.learningObjective: identify public compliance paired with private rejection
questions.stem: A participant gives the group's wrong answer aloud, then reports the correct one when alone in a booth. What does the pair show?

questions.topic: Social Psychology: Variables That Raise Normative Conformity
questions.learningObjective: identify which manipulation increases public agreement with a group
questions.stem: Which single change to a judgment task would most reliably raise the rate at which people give a wrong answer publicly?

answer.exemplar: The timing is what does the work. Once the choice is made and cannot be unmade, the reader is left holding two things that do not sit together: a preference for whichever book was better, and an awareness that the other was scarcer. A warning that arrives afterwards can only be used to build a bridge between them, so the reader finds a reason that makes the chosen book preferable, and the raised rating is that reason at work rather than a change in the book itself. The same information announced before the choice would not do this, because it would simply have entered the comparison as one more fact and the reader would have weighed scarcity against quality while both were still available. The reading is therefore not that the reader has become a better judge of the book, and not that the publisher has proved anything, but that an evaluation has been made to fit a decision that is already closed. Evidence for that reading would be a condition in which the reader is told the outcome only after committing, compared with one in which the same fact is available in advance: the divergence should appear in the first and not the second.

A person who has gone along aloud has a straightforward reason to have done so: the group is unanimous, disagreeing is visible, and standing out among several people costs something. A person who answers alone has no such reason and nothing to gain from dissembling, so their private answer is the better evidence of what they judge. An ability account says the groups differ on the test whatever they have been told beforehand, so it predicts a gap in the unwarned condition too. The warning account says the gap is produced by the warning, which means it should be absent when the same groups take the same test without being warned, and should appear when the warning is restored. First, the cost should be specific to the kind of task the stereotype describes, so the same participants should show little or no gap on an unrelated task taken in the same session. Second, the cost should be graded, with a group warned about a test they do poorly on showing a larger drop than one warned about a test they do well on. Against all of this the account should be treated cautiously rather than settled, because the size of the reported effect is disputed in the literature and a single group's result is weak evidence. A design that matched the groups on prior attainment, used the same test for both, and compared warned with unwarned participants within each group would be a fair test; a design comparing only two groups that differ in several ways at once would not be, whatever the difference looks like.

questions.explanation: The three terms differ in what the person is responding to, and the relation between them is nested rather than separate. Compliance is the broad case of yielding to a request without holding a view on it, and obedience is that case narrowed to a requester whose authority is recognised. Conformity is a different axis again, because it concerns matching a view held by others rather than answering a request at all. The pressure in conformity is also a specifically social one, which is why removing the audience removes it: a private answer has no audience to be managed for, and the agreement rate falls to a small residual. The tempting belief that the two differ by headcount fails because a crowd of equals is not a chain of command. The claim about a group directing a person as well as a superior fails because diffuse group pressure and recognised authority are different instruments.
questions.hint: Ask what each response is directed at: a request, an authority, or a group's shared view.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: Claims About Attribution Errors
questions.learningObjective: evaluate claims about the scope and relations of attribution errors
questions.stem: Four claims about attribution errors are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A person is given a situational excuse that an observer never receives, and that is part of the problem
The self-serving bias is found in groups as well as in individuals judging their own outcomes
Blaming a person for one act always amounts to calling them a stable bad character
options.misconception: conflates the locus of a cause with how long it is held to last

options.text: The false-consensus effect is simply the fundamental attribution error under another name
options.misconception: collapses two errors that concern different things entirely

questions.explanation: The first claim is the structural reason the error is systematic rather than occasional: the person performing an act has access to the pressures they are under, and the person watching usually does not, so the two are reasoning from different information and the observer's version is the thinner one. The second claim follows because the tendency to protect the self is not tied to a single body, and groups that win explain the win internally while explaining a loss externally behave the same way. The tempting belief that blaming always implies a stable bad character fails because locus and stability are separate dimensions, and a person can be judged responsible for one act without being written off. The claim that the false-consensus effect is the disposition error renamed fails because one concerns projecting a view onto others and the other concerns overweighting a trait against a situation, and neither is a special case of the other.
questions.hint: Check whether each claim concerns a bias about others, a bias about self, or a category mistake.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: The Steps in a Bystander's Decision
questions.learningObjective: order the steps by which a bystander reaches a decision not to act
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which they occur in the sequence that ends with nobody helping.

options.text: A bystander notices an unusual event and stops walking
The bystander tries to work out whether it amounts to a real emergency
The bystander checks how the other people nearby are responding to it
The bystander works out which of them ought to be the one to act
The bystander assumes one of those people will act and lets it pass

questions.explanation: Nothing can happen before the event is noticed, and the assessment of whether it is a real emergency comes before any use of other people, because until the bystander has decided the event needs doing there is no reason to consult anyone about it. The social check follows the assessment, and the allocation of the duty follows the social check, since the question of who should act only arises once the bystander has looked around and found other plausible candidates. The final step is the one the sequence is usually about: with several candidates identified and each assuming another will move, the bystander waits and the moment closes. The wrong order that puts the social check before the assessment fails because people look to others for cues about whether something is wrong, not for a verdict on their own interpretation. The wrong order that puts the assumption of someone else's action before the search fails because nobody is assumed to act until the search has produced candidates.
questions.hint: Start with what has to happen before any other person is even relevant, and end with the decision not to act.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: The Chain a Stereotype Warning Sets Off
questions.learningObjective: order the steps in the mechanism a stereotype warning is claimed to trigger
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which the claimed effect of a stereotype warning is supposed to unfold.

options.text: A group is told that its stereotype predicts poor performance on a particular test
Participants infer that a poor result would confirm what they have just been told
Anxiety rises and attention is partly spent monitoring their own performance
What is left for retrieving the material on the test is reduced by the monitoring
Accuracy falls, and the fall is largest on the test tied to the stereotype

questions.explanation: The chain has to start with the warning, since nothing downstream is set in motion without it, and the inference that a poor result would confirm the warning is what converts a piece of information into a reason to worry about one's own performance. The worry is what consumes attention, and the attention consumed by monitoring is attention taken away from the task itself, so the retrieval step has to come after the monitoring rather than alongside it. The accuracy drop is the outcome and the specificity claim is the final check on the account, since a cost that appeared on unrelated tasks as well would not be specific to the stereotype. The wrong order that puts retrieval before monitoring fails because there is nothing yet to compete with the task for attention. The wrong order that puts the accuracy fall before the retrieval cost fails because the cost is the proposed explanation of the fall, not a consequence of it.
questions.hint: Start with the event that has to occur before anything can be triggered, and treat the accuracy drop as the outcome.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: How an Effective Contact Sequence Runs
questions.learningObjective: order the structural steps a contact argument requires before change
questions.stem: Put these five events in the order in which they have to occur for contact to be credited with reducing dislike.

options.text: The two groups are placed in a setting where their standing is roughly equal
They are set a goal that both want and that neither would choose on its own
They have to combine their efforts to reach it, so each becomes dependent on the other
Each side acquires first-hand information that does not fit the stereotype it held
Mutual dislike falls, and the change is still there after the contact period ends

questions.explanation: The argument is structural, so the standing has to be settled first, since a shared goal offered to one side from a position of superiority is a favour rather than a joint aim and leaves the reasons for dislike intact. The goal comes next because dependence cannot be built without something both sides are trying to reach, and it is the need to combine efforts that turns two groups into collaborators rather than rivals under one roof. The informational step is the mechanism the whole arrangement exists to create, since personal contact is the only route by which the stereotype can be contradicted by the people it describes. The final step is the claim that matters, because a change that vanishes the moment the arrangement ends would not be a change in attitudes at all. The wrong order that puts the shared goal before equal standing fails because the goal is only shared in effect if the standing is comparable. The wrong order that puts the information before the dependence fails because the contact has to be cooperative before anything is learned about the other side.
questions.hint: Start with the condition that decides whether a shared goal is genuinely shared, and end with what happens after contact stops.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: One Bystander's Share of a Divided Duty
questions.learningObjective: compute one bystander's percentage share of an equally divided duty
questions.stem: A duty to intervene falls on four bystanders present, and each assumes it is shared equally between them. What percentage of the duty does one bystander hold?
questions.explanation: The duty is one whole and the four bystanders are assumed to share it equally, so each holds a quarter of it, which is 100 divided by 4, giving 25 percent. The figure matters because it is a per-person share rather than a group total: the group still holds all of the duty, but any individual within it holds a quarter, and that is the quantity a person is comparing against their own threshold for acting.
questions.hint: A quarter of a whole duty is 25 out of a hundred.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: Agreement Rate on Critical Trials
questions.learningObjective: convert a count of matching trials into a percentage rate
questions.stem: A participant answers 40 trials in which the group gives a wrong answer, and goes along with the group on 14 of those trials. What percentage of the critical trials were agreed with?
questions.explanation: The rate is the number of agreements divided by the number of critical trials, so 14 out of 40 is 14 divided by 40, which is 0.35, and expressed as a percentage that is 35 percent. The figure is only interpretable against the matching rate on non-critical trials, since the same participant's ordinary error rate is what the conformity figure has to be set beside.
questions.hint: Fourteen out of forty is a bit over a third of the trials.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Social Psychology: Percentage Shortening of a Response Time
questions.learningObjective: compute a percentage reduction from a before and after measurement
questions.stem: After a training programme the average time before a bystander reports an incident falls from 40 seconds to 25 seconds. By what percentage is the new figure shorter than the old one?
questions.explanation: The fall is 40 minus 25, which is 15 seconds, and a percentage reduction has the starting value as its denominator, so 15 out of 40 is 0.375, which is 37.5 percent. The same figure can be checked from the other end, because 25 out of 40 is 0.625, so the new value is 62.5 percent of the old one and must be 100 minus 62.5 percent shorter.
questions.hint: Find the drop of 15 seconds as a share of the 40 seconds it started at.
